name: Romanian deadlift
angleNote: Hip flexion: 0° = standing, 90° = trunk about horizontal. The knees bend a little as you hinge. Lifting makes the angle smaller. Torques are per leg; drag the figure to turn it.

strength.note: Relative isometric hip-extension torque vs hip flexion, peak about 53°, measured standing with the knee slightly bent (tested −29° to 74°; deeper hip flexion is held flat at the 74° value, which is extrapolation). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Relative isometric knee-extension torque vs knee flexion: weakest near full extension, peak about 65° (Anderson, tested 0–103°). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Lindahl et al. found the same shape (peak near 50°, about 50% of peak at 10°). Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022; Lindahl O, Movin A, Ringqvist I (1969/1972). Isometric knee extension strength as a function of joint angle, muscle length and motor unit activity. Acta Orthop Scand 43:138–147

negative.note: Knee flexion (negative torque: hamstrings and gastrocnemius pull the knee back). Anderson et al.'s knee-flexion curve and peak, as in the leg curl, measured seated with the hip at about 70°; corrected for the hip angle below.
negative.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Relative isometric plantarflexion torque vs plantarflexion (negative = dorsiflexed), peak about 23° of dorsiflexion, measured with the knee bent 50° (tested 29° dorsiflexion to 34° plantarflexion). Relative curve = cos(C2·(θ − C3)) with the 18–25-year-old male means of Table 3; points only inside the tested range, so the app holds the end values flat beyond it. Peak torque default from the same table's C1 (young men, scaled to 73 kg and 1.75 m).
strength.source: Anderson DE, Madigan ML, Nussbaum MA (2007). Maximum voluntary joint torque as a function of joint angle and angular velocity: model development and application to the lower limb. J Biomech 40(14):3105–3113. doi:10.1016/j.jbiomech.2007.03.022

strength.note: Hip adductor (positive) and abductor (negative) peak torque per leg, taken as constant across the range: Danneskiold-Samsøe et al.'s isometric means for healthy men aged 20–29 (lying on the side, knee straight, hip abducted 15–30°): adduction 217 Nm (SD 48), abduction 185 Nm (SD 38); women of the same age 124 and 114 Nm. Abductor strength falls as the hip abducts (Neumann et al.; Welsh et al.), which isn't modelled here. Earlier values from trained ice hockey players (Welsh et al.: 247 and 130 Nm) had a much larger adduction-to-abduction ratio. Both of Danneskiold-Samsøe et al.'s values sit at the top of the isometric datasets collected by Chen & Franklin (adduction roughly 0.5–1.3, abduction 0.5–1.0 Nm per kg·m of body mass × height), so the sideways efforts shown may be on the low side for an untrained lifter.
strength.source: Danneskiold-Samsøe B, Bartels EM, Bülow PM, Lund H, Stockmarr A, Holm CC, Wätjen I, Appleyard M, Bliddal H (2009). Isokinetic and isometric muscle strength in a healthy population with special reference to age and gender. Acta Physiol 197(Suppl 673):1–68. doi:10.1111/j.1748-1716.2009.02022.x (isometric hip adduction and abduction, men 20–29 years); previous values: Welsh P, Howitt S, Howarth SJ (2020). The influence of hip joint angle on the ratio between adduction and abduction torque in experienced, recreational male ice hockey players. Int J Sports Phys Ther 15(1):22–33. doi:10.26603/ijspt20200022; cross-check: Chen Z, Franklin DW (2025). Joint moment–angle/velocity relations in the hip, knee, and ankle: a meta-visualization of datasets. J Biomech 183 (read as the bioRxiv preprint, doi:10.1101/2024.06.22.600197, CC BY 4.0)

negative.note: Internal rotation (negative) by hip flexion: 25.2 Nm lying back (backrest 10°), 35.5 Nm at 55°, 39.4 Nm sitting (85°); it rises as the hip flexes (Uritani & Fukumoto). Held flat outside the tested range.
negative.source: Uritani D, Fukumoto T (2012). Differences of isometric internal and external hip rotation torques among three different hip flexion positions. J Phys Ther Sci 24(9):863–865 (Table 2: 20 students, 6 men and 14 women, isometric)

strength.note: External rotation (positive) by hip flexion: 36.5, 42.0 and 43.4 Nm with the backrest at 10°, 55° and 85° (Uritani & Fukumoto; the change wasn't significant). Hip flexion is taken as the backrest angle, which the authors didn't measure directly. The group (14 of 20 women, 60 kg on average) is lighter than this model's 75 kg man, so these are likely low for men; the strength slider scales them.
strength.source: Uritani D, Fukumoto T (2012). Differences of isometric internal and external hip rotation torques among three different hip flexion positions. J Phys Ther Sci 24(9):863–865 (Table 2: 20 students, 6 men and 14 women, isometric)

strength.note: No muscle capacity: a sideways knee moment is carried mostly by ligaments and the joint surfaces, so it is shown as torque only.
strength.source: Not applicable: carried by ligaments and joint surfaces, so no muscle strength is used

hip.note: Two-joint hamstrings: hip-extension strength by knee flexion, relative to the base curve's test (standing, knee slightly bent ≈ 15°). Yamamoto et al. measured 93 Nm with the knee bent 15° and 76 Nm at 90° (82%), with 2–3× more hamstring EMG at 15° and slightly more gluteus maximus at 90°. Measured prone with the hip straight, applied at every hip angle; held flat beyond the two knee angles. Other datasets found smaller (Chen & Franklin's collection: nearly flat) or larger (29–42%) differences.
hip.source: Yamamoto Y, Kato H, Fukuda T, Tsuga Y, Miyakawa S (2015). Effect of knee flexion angles during maximum isometric hip extension. Jpn J Phys Fitness Sports Med 64(3):289–294. doi:10.7600/jspfsm.64.289 (Fig. 2, read off: 93 Nm at 15° vs 76 Nm at 90° of knee flexion; 10 men, prone, hip straight)

ankle.note: Two-joint gastrocnemius: plantarflexion strength by knee flexion, relative to the base curve's test at 50° (Cresswell et al., Table 1: 134.9 Nm straight, 103.7 Nm at 90°, 80.4 Nm at 120°). A straight knee makes the calves about 20% stronger, a deep knee bend about 28% weaker.
ankle.source: Cresswell AG, Löscher WN, Thorstensson A (1995). Influence of gastrocnemius muscle length on triceps surae torque development and electromyographic activity in man. Exp Brain Res 105:283–290 (Table 1: 10 men, isometric, ankle 5° dorsiflexed)

knee.note: Two-joint hamstrings: knee-flexion strength by hip flexion, relative to the base curve's test at about 70° (Guex et al.: 62 Nm with the hip straight, 110 Nm at 90°, knee at 45°). Measured at one knee angle only.
knee.source: Guex K, Gojanovic B, Millet GP (2012). Influence of hip-flexion angle on hamstrings isokinetic activity in sprinters. J Athl Train 47(4):390–395. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.04 (Table: isometric, knee at 45°, 10 sprinters)

muscles.regionSharesNote: How the hamstrings' activity splits between the heads (close-up only): surface EMG during the stiff-leg deadlift (6 untrained men, 60% of body mass, knees straight), lifting phase: biceps femoris long head 43.5, semimembranosus 43, semitendinosus 33% of maximum (Fig. 1, read off), as fractions of the most active head. Lowering: 23, 28.7 and 17%, the semitendinosus again lowest. Other sources differ: an MRI study of the 45° back extension in women found the semitendinosus most active (Messer et al.), and turning the hips out shifts hip-extension work towards the biceps femoris (Park & Lim: 36 vs 18% of maximum). So the split depends on method, lift and stance.
muscles.regionSharesSource: Ono T, Higashihara A, Fukubayashi T (2011). Hamstring functions during hip-extension exercise assessed with electromyography and magnetic resonance imaging. Res Sports Med 19(1):42–52. doi:10.1080/15438627.2011.535769; Messer DJ, Bourne MN, Williams MD, Al Najjar A, Shield AJ (2018). Hamstring muscle use in women during hip extension and the Nordic hamstring exercise: a functional magnetic resonance imaging study. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 48(8):607–612. doi:10.2519/jospt.2018.7748; Park S, Lim W (2023). Comparison of muscle activity of hamstrings as knee flexors and hip extensors and effect of tibial and hip rotation on the contribution of hamstrings. J Bodyw Mov Ther 34:1–5. doi:10.1016/j.jbmt.2023.04.029
muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: Lengthened as you hinge with nearly straight knees: the main target of the lift.

muscles.name: Adductor magnus
muscles.note: Rear part extends the hip, more so when it is deeply bent.

muscles.name: Erector spinae
muscles.note: Hold the spine straight against a long lever. Approximation: driven by the hip's effort.

muscles.name: Calves (soleus, gastrocnemius)
muscles.note: Plantarflexors: keep the shin from tipping forward.

muscles.name: Adductors (longus, brevis, gracilis)
muscles.note: Work when the plate's push tends to spread the thighs apart: wide stances and toes out.

muscles.name: Gluteus medius and minimus
muscles.note: Work when the push tends to pull the thighs together: narrow stances, toes in.

muscles.name: Deep hip external rotators
muscles.note: Piriformis, obturators and gemelli (with the glutes) resist the thigh turning inwards.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Standing tall: the bar hangs close under the hips.

phases.name: Hinge
phases.text: Hips move back while the shins tilt back slightly so the bar stays over the mid-foot.

phases.name: Bottom
phases.text: Trunk near horizontal: the hip's moment arm is largest here.

variants.name: Barbell Romanian deadlift
variants.notes: Arms hang straight down from the shoulders. The solver tilts the shins so the centre of mass of body + bar stays over the mid-foot, which is what moves the hips back. Knee flexion grows from 5° to 23° through the hinge.

variants.name: Stiff-legged deadlift
variants.notes: Knees almost locked: the shins can't help, so the hips must travel further back and the hamstrings are stretched more.

variants.name: Wide stance, toes out
variants.notes: Feet wide and turned out. Hip extension stays about the same, but the feet now push outwards against the floor (least-effort estimate), which brings in the hip's sideways muscles. With the sideways push set to zero the adductors would have to hold the stance instead.

wger.name: Romanian Deadlift
wger.note: Checked against wger's public exercise list (id = the number in the page address).

momentArmNote: Moment arm = the joint's 3D distance from the floor's push line under that foot; it feeds every component of that joint's torque.

placement.label: Stance: each foot from the middle
Knees out (+) / in (−) of the toes
Feet push outwards against the floor (% of the vertical force)
